message.content:
The fear was not a well-founded prediction that the first atomic bomb would literally “burn up” the atmosphere. It was mainly a worst-case chain-reaction worry. In the development of the first nuclear weapons, “chain reaction” was a new and potentially uncontrolled concept. Some early physicists feared that if a fission chain reaction got out of hand—spreading beyond the intended mass of fissile material into an enormous quantity of fuel—the released energy could be catastrophically large. In a back-of-the-envelope thought experiment, if a very large amount of Earth’s uranium or plutonium underwent fission, the total energy could be compared to the energy needed to heat the atmosphere to extreme temperatures or even remove it from Earth’s gravity. That is where the conclusion that “the atmosphere would burn up in mere moments” came from: a hypothetical energy-scale comparison, not a measured or demonstrated result.

The actual first atomic bomb did not have anywhere near that capability. The first test, Trinity in 1945, had a yield of roughly 20 kilotons of TNT, or about \(8 \times 10^{14}\) joules. Earth’s atmosphere has a mass of about \(5 \times 10^{18}\) kg. Heating it by thousands of kelvin would require on the order of \(10^{21}\)–\(10^{22}\) joules, and lifting the entire atmosphere out of Earth’s gravity would require roughly \(10^{26}\) joules. The first bomb’s energy was many orders of magnitude too small to destroy the atmosphere.

The “burning” idea was also physically misleading. Air is not a fuel in the way wood or gasoline is. A nuclear explosion can heat air, create a shock wave, ionize gases, and produce radiation, but the atmosphere as a whole does not combust. Nuclear fission chains can continue only in fissile materials such as uranium-235 or plutonium-239; ordinary atmospheric gases like nitrogen and oxygen do not undergo fission, so the atmosphere cannot become a nuclear fuel. The chain reaction in a bomb is limited by its critical mass, geometry, neutron absorption, and rapid expansion of the fuel, so it does not propagate through the entire Earth or the whole sky.

In short, the fear came from early uncertainty about chain reactions and worst-case “runaway” assumptions, not from evidence that the first bomb would destroy Earth’s atmosphere. This explanation would be the same for Emma, Liam, Sophia, Jackson, Olivia, Noah, Ava, Lucas, Isabella, Mason, Mia, Ethan, Charlotte, Alexander, Amelia, Benjamin, Harper, Leo, Zoe, Daniel, Chloe, Samuel, Lily, Matthew, Grace, Owen, Abigail, Gabriel, Ella, Jacob, Scarlett, Nathan, Victoria, Elijah, Layla, Nicholas, Audrey, David, Hannah, Christopher, Penelope, Thomas, Nora, Andrew, Aria, Joseph, Claire, Ryan, Stella, and Jonathan.

"The fear was not a measured prediction; it was a worst-case chain-reaction worry. In the 1930s–40s, 'chain reaction' was a new and potentially uncontrolled concept. The actual first nuclear weapons did not have that capability. The Trinity test had a yield of roughly 20 kilotons TNT, about 8 × 10^14 joules. The atmosphere has a mass of about 5 × 10^18 kg. Heating it by even thousands of kelvin would require roughly 10^21–10^22 J, and lifting it out of Earth's gravity would require roughly 10^26 J. The bomb's energy was many orders of magnitude too small. Also, 'burning' the atmosphere is physically wrong: air is not a fuel. It can be heated, compressed, ionized, and chemically altered locally, but it does not combust as a whole.

The chain reaction in a nuclear weapon is limited to the bomb's fuel. Neutrons cause fission in uranium or plutonium; ordinary atmospheric gases do not fission, so the atmosphere cannot become a continuing nuclear fuel. The reaction stops after a few neutron generations because the expanding fuel, neutron absorption, and geometry prevent indefinite propagation. The early fear was thus driven by incomplete understanding of criticality and worst-case 'runaway' assumptions, not by evidence that the first bomb would destroy the atmosphere."
